title-info.genre: Isekai dark fantasy with LitRPG progression

annotation.p: Aetheria is a sprawling high-fantasy realm whose laws of physics, magic, and life itself are not born from gods or nature but maintained by the System—a vast, failing world-enchantment that functions like corrupted server code. Floating glyphs materialize above every soul's head displaying levels, stats, and quest logs; dungeons spawn from overwritten data tables; monsters flicker in and out of existence when their descriptions desynchronize. The air hums with unstable enchantment energy, and reality occasionally glitches—gravity inverts for blocks that walk through doors, colors bleed into impossible spectrums, and NPCs repeat dialogue loops when the System misallocates memory. This is a world where magic obeys syntax, dungeons are procedurally generated from broken entries, and corruption spreads like a virus eating the boundaries between rules.

section.p: The rain tasted wrong—not cold, not wet, but like biting into a fresh circuit board. It fell as individual streams of liquid light that fractured when they struck my skin, each droplet resolving briefly into scrolling hexadecimal before evaporating back into mist. I gasped and pulled myself upright from the puddle on the pavement, water dripping from my knuckles so violently my hands shook.

Above my left shoulder hung a jagged glyph interface, half-dissolving in the neon haze: Level 1, Class: Glitch-Walker (Undeclared), Health 87/87, Ability: Admin Terminal Access [Passive]. The text flickered like a dying monitor’s backlight. I knew that layout from somewhere—perhaps a training sim back home before my heart stopped, or the afterlife queue where souls were processed through automated soulware. Details didn’t matter. What mattered was how the rain around me continued to stutter; each drop refused to fall straight down anymore, orbiting micro-second loops before committing to gravity’s pull.

I stood on wobbly legs, vision swimming with static that looked suspiciously like a corrupted video feed. This wasn’t a hospital room. The street stretched away in both directions as part of Edge District, the border town between the proper city and the Corrupted Spire dungeon zone where reality broke down into raw data tables. Neon signs buzzed overhead with looping sale dialogs—"50% OFF ENCHANTED BREAD"—and every third streetlamp inverted gravity for three seconds before snapping back to normal. I’d seen this glitch pattern in server logs, usually indicating a memory leak at the heap allocator. Reality here ran on someone else’s bad code.

A sound cut through the rain: wet clicking, like fingers scraping down glass. I froze. Behind me, shadows pooled in the gutter—too many of them, moving independently from their sources. Shadow-stalkers flickered into existence out of corrupted data tables; their bodies assembled from fragments of darkness and missing geometry. They had no faces, only hollow sockets where eyes should be, their limbs clicking together at angles that shouldn’t exist in three-dimensional space. One lunged for my ankle with a speed that defied its own physics.

I moved before I thought about moving, my body reacting on pure instinct. The stalker’s claw met my boot with a sickening crunch. Instead of pain, what registered was an error—a segmentation fault between perception and sensation. Above my head the glyphs pulsed red: Health 85/87. A shadow had taken its toll, but I barely felt it.
"PATCH LOCAL ENTITIES TO STABLE STATE," I whispered. The words left me like a reflex, like typing a command line prompt you’d punched in ten thousand times over in your life.

The stalker froze mid-lunge, its form glitching as if caught on a corrupted texture map. Around me the air hummed with static, and all five of them stuttered into coherent shape—no longer mindless hunger engines but hollow puppets waiting for their next instruction. Their aggression codes had been recalibrated to zero by my voice alone. I’d spent two days in a hospital bed before dying; three years as a senior systems administrator at CloudCore Infrastructure before cardiac arrest took me home. Now reality itself responded to admin edicts spoken aloud.

But there was a cost. Health 83/87. The shadow-stalkers hadn’t been the only things connected to this area’s data stream. Some fragment of the System had deducted penalty damage for unauthorized code execution, or maybe it was just the world balancing its own books. I didn’t have time to figure out which before the sound came again—this time closer, heavier, like metal dragging over stone.
I ran.

The alley behind me twisted in on itself as I passed through, walls brushing my shoulders with damp brick that felt simultaneously solid and translucent, like touching a hologram at too close range. The rain had stopped somewhere between the main street and here; instead came a thick fog of blue static that tasted metallic against my tongue. Every few meters reality would glitch—a door frame extending into three dimensions before snapping back flat, a shop window displaying a frozen image from yesterday’s inventory, a pigeon’s feather dissolving into ASCII text mid-air before reforming as normal keratin.

I knew this place because I’d read its logs once, in the System’s peripheral data vaults where deleted patches and corrupted entries were stored like grave dust. Archivist Nyx called it "the dead edge." Nobody stayed long here—the System treated Edge District as low-priority memory to be recycled whenever its corruption rate spiked above acceptable thresholds. Most people who ended up on this side of the border didn’t leave without getting caught in a purge sweep and deleted permanently.

The alley opened onto a small plaza where three merchants were clustered around a broken vending machine that kept dispensing half-finished potions instead of completing their recipes. Kaelen Rostov stood at the edge of it all, leaning against a brick wall with his hands deep in his pockets. He wore a leather jacket patched together from discarded UI fragments and what looked like corrupted armor plating, his hair streaked with neon blue static that drifted through the fog around him.

He froze when I approached, eyes narrowing behind cracked spectacles. His gaze flickered over me—the floating stat block above my head, the slight shimmer in my clothes where reality refused to fully render around me—and then something changed in his expression. Not fear. Recognition. A sort of cold curiosity that made my stomach turn.

"You’re not just bleeding code anymore," he said, stepping into the dim light with a grin that didn’t quite reach his eyes. He held out a hand that smelled of ozone and cheap tobacco smoke—the scent of someone who’d been smoking through terminal burns for years. "You patched them, didn’t you?"

I stopped at the edge of his personal space, still catching my breath. Health 79/87 by now—somehow I’d taken more damage in the last thirty seconds than in the previous two days combined. The shadow-stalkers had been easy. What came next would probably kill me outright if I wasn’t careful about how many admin edicts I threw around before someone started asking questions.
"I don’t know what you’re talking about," I said, keeping my voice flat. "I’m just—"

Kaelen cut in with a sharp laugh that echoed off the damp walls. "You patched three shadow entities into stable form within seconds of materializing. That’s not just bleeding code anymore, Mik. That’s direct interaction at source level." He pushed off from the wall and gestured toward the merchants’ stall with one hand. "And you did it without triggering a purge sweep—which means your edicts are subtle enough to pass as natural system behavior."

I didn’t respond; I kept watching him, analyzing his stance against the static-laden fog. Kaelen had the posture of someone used to moving through cracks in the architecture of things. His boots were scuffed, not from walking on stone but from dragging across corrupted textures.

"I’ve been farming this spot for six months," he said, continuing as if my silence was expected. "While they desync their inventory loops every thirty minutes. I get about forty percent of what drops because most of it gets flagged as corrupted loot and sent straight to the void." He glanced at me again, that cold curiosity sharpening into something almost like respect. "You just stabilized the zone long enough for me to collect the rest."
"Then you’re welcome," I said, unsure why my voice sounded so tired. "I didn’t come here to help anyone."

Kaelen tilted his head, studying me with an expression that could have been anything—interest, calculation, or maybe just fatigue. "We both know you did," he said finally. He reached into his jacket and pulled out a small, rectangular object wrapped in static-cling plastic: a corrupted quest key from the vending machine merchant’s glitched inventory loop. "I’ll give you this one free."

He tossed it into my hand before I could respond. The object hummed faintly against my palm, warm like someone had just opened their mouth to speak. Above my head the glyphs flickered again—Health 78/87, but now with a new line appearing beneath it: Ability Cooldown Resetting [29s].

"What happens when you ask me why?" Kaelen asked quietly, his gaze fixed on the fog beyond the alley walls where the system’s corruption rate seemed to spike and drop in irregular patterns. "You’re not exactly invisible right now."

I looked down at my hand, then back up at him. The plaza stretched out between us for what felt like miles, but I knew it was only fifty meters across—the distance from one brick building to another when reality refused to follow Euclidean geometry anymore. Above Kaelen’s head hung his own stat block: Level 15 Rogue (Glitch-Exploiter), Health 142/142, Quest Active: ???

"Heads up," he said without looking at me, glancing toward the edge of vision where something massive was moving through the fog—too big to be a dungeon monster, too deliberate in its path. "You’re going to want that ability cooldown reset if you’re going to keep using it." He turned back fully then, his grin sharper this time, edged with genuine amusement. "And don’t worry about paying me back for the key. I’m not greedy enough to ask for gold from someone who talks to reality like he’s running a server farm."

The massive shape passed through our line of sight and dissolved into mist before we could see what it was—probably a patrol entity checking corruption rates, or maybe something else entirely that had been deleted from the official logs long ago. I watched it go without realizing I’d stopped breathing until the fog cleared enough to remember where my lungs were located.

Kaelen waited five seconds, then shrugged and turned back toward the plaza’s edge where a few street vendors were setting up stalls with glitching inventory displays that showed different items depending on who looked at them. "Come on," he said over his shoulder. "If you’re going to be around long enough to figure out how your powers work without getting purged, I can show you the best places in Edge District where reality’s most likely to crack."

Kaelen didn't look at me when he spoke. He was already scanning a desynced loot drop three streets over—glowing gear floating in midair where a skeleton merchant had flickered out of sync with its corpse table—and his voice came from behind me, calm and clipped.
"Don't waste it," he said. "Not on little things."

I froze, still standing near the plaza's edge where I'd neutralized those shadow-stalkers with my first instinctive command: PATCH LOCAL ENTITIES TO STABLE STATE. My throat felt tight; my palms burned with the ghost of static discharge. A cooldown bar appeared above my vision—thin red line beneath a translucent icon that looked like an open terminal window. It was already receding, slowly but steadily filling back up in increments of three percent per heartbeat.
"What is it?" I asked. "The timer? Does it reset on use?"

Kaelen tossed me a small, irregular shard of black glass—it pulsed with erratic violet glyphs that hurt my eyes if I stared too long. A corrupted quest key. He caught the look in them and snatched it back before I could reach for it.
"Cooldowns aren't timers," he said. "They're currency. You spend one edict to stabilize a collapsed doorframe, and you don't get it back until you've paid the interest."

He gestured toward the nearest flickering building—a two-story structure whose windows occasionally displayed looping advertisement loops for guild recruitment. A group of goblins was clustered around its base, arguing over a dropped bag that kept sliding through their feet instead of being claimed. Gravity had desynced on it; physics tables were corrupted to local consistency errors.

"If you want to cross the Spire fringe," Kaelen continued, "you can't just spray fixes everywhere. The System notices unauthorized edits. It weaponizes them." He stepped closer, his patched leather coat crinkling like a dead screen saver. "Think about it: you walk through here and every time you stabilize something—fix a glitched door, patch a corrupted mob's aggression flag—the system logs your signature as 'repair activity.' Repair signatures are the bait."
A chill that had nothing to do with the damp wind slid down my spine.

"Repair signatures attract Purge Drones," Kaelen said flatly. "Your first instinct was right: when you whispered that command, I saw what happened to the shadow-stalkers. Their code bled out of sync and collapsed into harmless data fragments because your edit forced them into a state where the System recognized them as stable again." He paused. "But Purge Drones don't care about stability. They hunt anomalies. And a sudden patch in a dead zone? That's an anomaly screaming for deletion."

I looked down at my hands. The red cooldown line was still thin—only forty percent recovered since I'd spoken the command. I hadn't even realized I had such limited capacity; until now, I'd assumed edicts could be chained like spells, stacked and layered without consequence. Kaelen was right: it felt less like magic and more like accessing a privileged terminal with a single-use token attached to every keystroke.
"Show me," I said.

Kaelen smirked, that sharp, cynical curl of his lips. "You want a lesson in economy? Fine." He pointed toward the plaza's central fountain—a monolith of cracked marble and pulsing light where water kept cycling through states: liquid, steam, binary static, and occasionally pure void. At its base sat a cluster of NPCs whose health bars hovered between life and death. They weren't hostile; they were simply stuck in a procedural loop that had never been patched out.
"Stabilize one," Kaelen said. "Use your edict on the fountain's central glyph. Just one. Then tell me what you see."

I stepped forward, closing my eyes for a heartbeat to clear the static buzzing at the edges of my vision. When I opened them again, the glyph above the fountain pulsed with corrupted orange light—its description table was desynced; it displayed multiple conflicting health values and quest flags simultaneously. I could feel the pull of the command forming in my throat: a reflexive impulse to reach out and smooth the jagged edges.
I spoke instead, carefully choosing the syntax this time rather than letting instinct drive me. "PATCH LOCAL ENTITY TO STABLE STATE."

The glyph flared white-hot for an instant, then settled into a clean blue pulse. The fountain's water stopped cycling; it became still liquid again. Above my head, the red cooldown line dropped by exactly fifteen percent in exchange for that single, precise edit. No more than I had spent on the shadow-stalkers.

Kaelen nodded once, satisfied. "See? You don't use edicts to fix everything. You use them to make sure nothing breaks when you need it most." He gestured toward the Spire's outer wall—a jagged silhouette of corrupted geometry that loomed just beyond the plaza like a broken monument. The air near it hummed with unstable enchantment energy, and floating glyphs flickered in and out of existence as if reality itself were buffering. "We're heading there now. Past those walls is where the corruption thickens into physical debris—where rules stop being suggestions and start being obstacles."

I hesitated. Kaelen had made his position clear: he didn't care about loyalty or morality, only utility. His alliance was transactional, built on the mutual recognition that we both existed in a gray zone between features and bugs. But something about his warning lingered—the idea that my very ability to edit reality could be turned against me.
"Are we safe?" I asked. "If we're not triggering Purge Drones now..."

Kaelen's expression tightened, just for a moment—something darker than cynicism flickered beneath it. "Safe is a relative term in Edge District," he said. "But you're right: the deeper we go past those walls, the more unstable reality becomes. And the more your cooldowns matter." He turned toward me, his eyes glinting with something that might have been respect or might have been calculation. "The Spire's outer fringe is where System memory status drops to low-priority. That's why I've been farming here—loot spawns faster when the garbage collector forgets what it should be deleting." He paused. "You'll learn to treat cooldowns like currency, Mik. And you'll learn that every edict costs more than you think."

We moved toward the wall together, stepping through zones where gravity occasionally inverted for three seconds and colors bled into impossible spectrums—a streetlight turned purple for no reason, then snapped back; a patch of grass flickered into wireframe mesh before dissolving into static. The environment felt less like reality and more like a poorly patched simulation holding itself together by sheer inertia.
At the checkpoint—a broken archway carved from corrupted basalt where floating glyphs displayed fragmented quest logs that repeated in endless loops—we were intercepted.

She materialized out of thin air, or at least out of the static that clung to everything around us. Elena Voss was a spectral figure wrapped in shifting layers of glitched UI fragments; half her body resolved into coherent form while the rest remained as translucent overlay patterns and looping dialogue text. She wore armor that looked like it had been ripped from a System-generated quest reward, now decayed into mismatched plates and corrupted engravings.

"You're leaking repair signatures," she said, her voice layered with distortion—part of it clear, part of it repeating in a loop: *...patch signature detected... anomaly flagged...* "Kaelen can see them coming too." She gestured to the Spire wall behind us, where three large mechanical shapes were coalescing from the darkness—Purge Drones. Their forms were sleek and angular, constructed of black metal and glowing red glyphs that pulsed in synchronization with their movement. They hadn't attacked yet; they were simply assembling, drawn by the faint trail our unauthorized edits had left behind.
Kaelen cursed under his breath, already pulling a jagged shard of corrupted glass from his belt—a weapon made entirely of unstable data fragments. "Damn it," he muttered. "She's here."

Elena turned her gaze toward me. Her eyes flickered—sometimes human brown, sometimes raw code. She took a half-step forward and the air around us cracked like thin ice; reality stuttered as if the System had momentarily lost its grip on local physics.
"You're not just noticed," she said, "you're weaponized."
"Explain," I said. My voice sounded small in the humming static of the checkpoint zone.

"The first time you spoke an edict," Elena continued, her coherence flickering—her form dissolving into a cascade of floating glyphs for three seconds before snapping back together, "the System registered it as unauthorized repair activity. It logged your signature and immediately broadcast it through the enchantment's maintenance network." She paused, looking at Kaelen with something that might have been pity or warning. "That's how you survived the shadow-stalkers: they were corrupted entities in a dead zone where nothing was actively monitored. But now? Now your existence is flagged as 'anomalous repair source.' The System doesn't just track it; it uses it."

A Purge Drone detached itself from the wall and glided toward us, its red glyphs blazing like warning lights. Kaelen threw his corrupted glass shard at it without hesitation. The shard passed through the drone's body, disrupting its synchronization tables for an instant. The drone stumbled, glitching into a brief loop where it repeated its approach motion three times before snapping back to normal and accelerating again.

"See?" Elena said, her voice sharp now, cutting through the static. "Your edicts create repair signatures that Purge Drones track like prey. Every patch you make is a beacon. And they're getting closer." She pointed toward the Spire wall—three more drones had coalesced from the shadows, their forms larger and more advanced than the first.

Kaelen glanced at me, his expression unreadable for the briefest moment before settling into grim determination. "Then we patch harder," he said. "We make sure your cooldowns don't run dry in the middle of a sweep." He turned back toward Elena. "You can help us mask those signatures if you want to survive this."
Elena's form flickered violently again, her edges dissolving into cascading glyphs and looping dialogue text that repeated: *...stabilizing anchor required... coherence buffer failing...*

"I need an anchor," she said, her voice straining now, half of it clear and the other half bleeding through as corrupted data. "A stabilizing anchor to bind my fragmented buffers together long enough for me to interface with your patch signatures and mask them from the System's purge protocols." She looked at Kaelen, then at me. Her coherence was failing faster; more of her body resolved into static overlays. "You have the capacity to create stable zones—your edicts force local reality into a consistent state. That consistency is what I need."

Kaelen swore again, louder this time. He was already scanning the drones' movement patterns, calculating angles and escape routes. Elena's warning hung heavy in the air: our very survival depended on understanding how the System used unauthorized edits as bait for its own cleanup mechanisms. We were walking into a trap of our own making—and we had no idea how deep it went.
"You're telling me," I said slowly, "that every time I fix something here, I'm not just editing reality? I'm handing the System an invitation?"

Elena nodded once, her form flickering through states: human woman, spectral glyph construct, and occasionally nothing at all before snapping back together. "The enchantment that holds this world—this 'System' you're discovering—isn't just corrupted code," she said. Her voice dropped lower now, almost a whisper despite the drones circling closer still. "It's a countermeasure built to contain something worse than corruption."

Kaelen froze, his weapon halfway raised. I could see it in how he went rigid—how every muscle locked into defensive posture as if expecting an ambush from nowhere. Elena's voice cut through the static like a blade. "The enchantment isn't protecting Aetheria's inhabitants. It's containing something that feeds on instability itself."

Another drone detached from the wall, its red glyphs blazing brighter than before. Kaelen exhaled sharply and shoved me toward him. "Move!" he yelled over the crackling hum of destabilized reality. He threw his corrupted glass shard at the nearest drone; it passed through harmlessly this time—the drone's synchronization tables were already destabilizing from Elena's proximity, her presence acting as a localized glitch bomb.

As we sprinted past the checkpoint toward the Spire wall, I felt the first true weight of what Kaelen had been warning me about: every edict I'd cast since awakening left a trail, and now that trail was drawing hunters instead of stabilizing zones. The red cooldown line above my vision pulsed steadily as I ran, counting down my remaining capacity. And beyond the wall—the jagged silhouette of corrupted geometry looming like a broken monument—lay something far older than corruption itself. Something that had built this enchantment not to protect us, but to keep whatever was behind it from noticing we were finally awake enough to make noise.

Elena's words echoed in my mind as the drones closed in: *It feeds on instability.* And I realized with a cold certainty that our very existence here—our unauthorized edits, our glitch-walking partnership, our fragile foothold in this corrupted border zone—was fuel for something far worse than decay.

The air tasted of ozone and burnt sugar as the Warden swept through the Edge District again. It wasn't a creature—it was an architecture of light and judgment, moving in perfect geometric arcs across the sky while its voice broadcast from every flickering streetlamp:
*UNAUTHORIZED REPAIR SIGNATURES DETECTED. PURGE PROTOCOL ENGAGED.*

Three blue-white drones descended from the shimmering haze above, their hulls etched with glyphs that shifted between Latin and dead languages. They hummed a frequency that made my teeth ache and fractured vision into wireframe segments. Kaelen's eyes went wide behind his cracked goggles as he spun around, jagged shards of corrupted glass already drawn. Elena materialized at our flank—a spectral figure wrapped in static, her form flickering like a loading screen stuck on ninety percent.
"Run," she said, voice layered with the echo of ten thousand dialogue loops. "They're rewriting physics."

That was when the first trap closed. The drone hovering above the cobblestones emitted a pulse—not sonic, not magical, but something deeper: a direct injection into local reality code. Gravity inverted for three blocks in every direction simultaneously. Shops hung suspended upside down, raindrops fell upward through open storefronts, and civilians screamed as their bodies refused to follow the new vector.
I didn't hesitate. I spent ten percent of my cooldown—and spoke: "PATCH LOCAL VECTORS TO ORIGINAL STATE."

Reality shivered like a corrupted save file reloading. The inverted blocks snapped back into alignment. Shop signs dropped with wet thuds. A merchant's cart rolled sideways, spilling produce onto the street in slow motion before catching its wheels again. But as I completed the edict, three red glyphs burned themselves above my head:
*COOLDOWN ACTIVE. ESTIMATED RETURN: 4 MINUTES 12 SECONDS.* *SIGNATURE TRACE DETECTED BY WARDEN PROTOCOL.* *TIER-ONE ACCESS RESTRICTED.*
"They're tracking me," I muttered.
Elena's static form pulsed brighter, her spectral hands reaching toward my chest. "You need to bind them before they lock the gates."
"Bind what?"

"The breach," she said, voice cutting through the drone hum. "Your repairs create a measurable anomaly in the containment field. If you don't stabilize it now, the Warden won't just hunt you—it'll quarantine the entire district."

The drones moved faster now, their blue-white light intensifying as they synchronized. Kaelen hurled one of his glass shards at the lead drone, watching it shatter into fragmented pixels that dissolved before hitting the target. "Nice try," he called over the static. "You can't out-glitch a full-spectrum purge."

I had about three percent left in my cooldown. Enough for one precise edit. Not enough to stop the Warden. But maybe... just maybe... I could buy time. I needed them close to the Spire wall, where reality was already thin, corrupted, and unstable—where the System's own defenses would interfere with its pursuit algorithms.
"Kaelen," I said, voice low. "Can you draw them away? Use your glitch-loopholes."
The rogue grinned despite the danger. "You got it." He sprinted toward the nearest drone cluster, arms spread like an invoker welcoming a death sentence.

As they engaged, Elena stepped forward, her spectral hands pressing against my chestplate where I could feel no bone beneath. It burned cold, and for a moment reality itself stuttered—the street tiles turned into wireframe cubes before snapping back to solid stone. "I need your anchor," she whispered, static crackling around us like a dying transmitter.
"What do you mean?"

"Your edict binds me temporarily," Elena said, her eyes glowing with fragmented light. "Just long enough for me to mask your signature in the audit logs. But it costs me stability." Her form flickered violently as she absorbed part of my cooldown into herself—a dangerous exchange that left her even more transparent than before.
"Good," I said, though my stomach knotted at what she was offering. "Now hold on tight."
The Warden's voice came through every surface now, omnidirectional and absolute: *TARGET IDENTIFIED. CONTAINMENT BREACH DETECTED. INITIATING FINAL PURGE SEQUENCE.*

The three blue-white drones converged in a perfect triangle formation, their glyphs turning from red to an angry white-hot. They weren't just hunting me anymore—they were executing a system-level deletion command on the entire block.
That was when the fracture hit.

Reality tore open above us—a jagged wound in the world that revealed not sky or darkness, but raw code flowing like liquid mercury beneath the enchantment's skin. The fracture expanded with terrifying speed, swallowing storefronts, pavement, anything within its reach. People screamed as their bodies desynchronized from reality, flickering between solid and translucent before dissolving into static.

I could feel my own edges fraying—my stats, my cooldown bars, even the memories of this morning becoming unstable. I had to do something drastic. Something the System would flag as a Tier-Three violation.
"Kaelen!" I shouted over the tearing world. "Get them close to that alley behind the apothecary! There's a registry entry there—"

The fracture swallowed my words before I could finish, and then it closed with a sound like breaking glass on an infinite scale. We were back in the street—mostly—but the geometry was wrong now. Buildings leaned at impossible angles, windows showed reflections from three seconds ago instead of now, and the sky pulsed between dawn purple and midnight black in looping cycles.
"Damn," Kaelen said, wiping blood from his lip as he landed heavily beside us. "You broke something big."
Elena was gone—dissolved into pure static that scattered across the pavement like shattered pixels. A new glyph burned above my head:
*TIER-THREE ACCESS GRANTED.* *FULL-BLOCK STABILIZATION ACTIVE (DURATION: INFINITE)* *PERMANENT SIGNATURE TRACE LOGGED TO SYSTEM AUDIT.* *WARDEN PROTOCOL ELEVATING PRIORITY.*

I could feel it humming through me—the power of editing entire blocks of reality as a single command, the ability to bind syntax fragments together in ways that would make even Elena's guardians cringe. But I also felt the System watching, tracking every meter of stabilization I'd forced into existence. My repairs were no longer hidden anomalies; they were documented violations written in permanent ink across the audit logs.

"We need to move," Kaelen said, already scanning the cracked buildings around us. "But straight up? Straight down?" He pointed toward the Spire wall that loomed ahead, where reality was so corrupted that gravity occasionally fired shots of pure force against anyone who stepped too close. "That's your best bet. The registry entry I mentioned—it's near a desynced data vault under the archway. You can hide your signature there for a while."
"Hide my signature?" I echoed, feeling the weight of Elena's warning settling over me like lead armor.

"She said containment breach," Kaelen replied. "And you know what that means. The System is accelerating its response because it actually *measured* what you did today. That's not normal purge behavior." He glanced at where Elena had stood, then back to the Spire wall with something like fear. "You're going in there, Mik. Not for loot. Not for quests. You need answers about why it fights back so hard."

The Warden's voice returned, louder now, echoing through every surface: *PROXY TARGET IDENTIFIED. INITIATING CONTAINMENT PROTOCOLS.* The streetlights above us flickered and died one by one, plunging the district into emergency amber glow from backup generators that also seemed to be glitching out of sync.

I looked down at my hands. They were steady now, no longer trembling with the shock of rebirth or the adrenaline of survival. I had something more than raw power—I had access to a tier of command syntax most System administrators would kill for. And it had cost me everything in permanent exposure.
"Kaelen," I said quietly. "Help me get into that vault under the archway. We're going deep."

The rogue nodded, already moving toward where reality thinnest and the Spire's corrupted geometry stretched like torn fabric across the horizon. Behind us, the Warden continued its sweep, blue-white drones rewriting physics one block at a time while civilians huddled in doorways too afraid to flee what was clearly not nature but something far worse: architecture that learned how to hunt.

I followed him toward the Spire wall, my Tier-Three access humming in sync with every corrupted glyph I passed. The containment breach had been measured now—and it was accelerating. There were answers down there, buried beneath layers of deleted patches and pre-collapse logs that Elena's fragmented memories had hinted at once. And if I wanted to understand why reality itself turned against me the moment I tried to fix it, I needed to see what lay waiting in the dark beyond the wall.
We moved forward into the fracture zone where physics forgot its job and the System finally showed teeth.

The archway hummed beneath my fingertips—a frequency that vibrated in bone rather than air, like standing too long near a server rack overheating under load. Kaelen had pointed at the warped geometry where reality bent like cheap plastic: three doors stacked vertically instead of horizontally, floor tiles displaying rotating quest markers unassigned to any player or monster within ten miles, and the occasional shard of solidified light floating mid-air as if someone had spilled a glass of starlight.

"Desynced data vault," Kaelen muttered, his voice cracking against the architecture like dry glass. He adjusted one of the UI fragments stitched into his shoulder pauldron; it flickered red then blue. "This is where they store patches that never got deployed. If anyone's hiding anything from the purge logs, it's in here."

The corridor beyond our starting point was no longer a corridor—walls leaned at impossible angles, ceiling glyphs displayed corrupted hex code scrolling faster than eyes could read, and floor tiles shifted beneath us like sand under boots not worn for decades. I placed my palm against the nearest wall; it resisted like cold steel but felt warm in my grip, as if something had recently touched it.
"Tier-Three access," I said aloud, testing the boundaries of my remaining permissions. "Generate a local diagnostic overlay."

Nothing appeared above my head—no stat block, no cooldown meter. But the air around us stuttered. The flickering door markers froze mid-rotation, the scrolling hex halted at a single repeating line: `WARN: STRUCTURAL INTEGRITY BELOW THRESHOLD`. Reality hiccuped—a half-second pause where gravity felt optional—and then we were sliding down it.

"Keep your footing," Kaelen shouted over the groan of shifting architecture. "This place rewrites its own generation table hourly. You walk fast enough, you're in a different dungeon by the time you reach the other end."

We descended through a stairwell that spiraled into darkness without getting darker—light sources materialized from thin air like corrupted textures loading in an engine gone wrong: floating spheres of pale white glow, some flickering between transparency and blinding intensity. I kept my edicts to myself; each use left a signature. Each repair generated heat that attracted something hunting for it. But the corridor was growing tighter—walls compressing inward as if trying to close a file too large to open—and I could feel the Spire's procedural engine humming beneath our feet like a sleeping predator shifting in its den.

At the base of the stairwell, we found an atrium where geometry had already begun breaking down into abstract shapes: floating cubes drifting through air as if testing gravity parameters, doorways that existed only when viewed from certain angles, and a central pillar of obsidian-black material pulsing with red glyphs identical to those on the Purge Drones.
"Core chamber," Kaelen said, his voice dropping to something almost respectful beneath the static in his hair. "That's where Nyx sleeps."

The obsidian pillar had no face; only a surface that rippled like water disturbed by wind. Around it floated glyphs—not stats or quest markers—but raw data fragments: pre-collapse logs, corrupted patches, entries marked for deletion but never purged. I could feel my Tier-Three access extending into them like roots seeking moisture in dry earth.
"Show me what you know," I said. "About why the System escalates containment when repairs are made."

Kaelen stepped back from the pillar. "You're asking Nyx?" He glanced at the glyphs, his expression unreadable for the first time since we'd met at the archway. "He doesn't talk unless he has data to trade."

The obsidian surface rippled faster now, red glyphs cycling into a sequence I recognized from Elena's fragmented memories: `CONTAINMENT PROTOCOL ACTIVE`, followed by `THREAT VECTORS DETECTED`. Something about my presence was triggering a response—not in me, but through me. The pillar hummed louder, and for a second I saw not data but faces forming within the glyph patterns: architects? Guardians? Something older watching from behind their own code.
"Use your access," Kaelen said quietly. "But don't patch it."

I nodded and let my Tier-Three permissions bleed into the pillar's surface, extending diagnostic queries rather than applying edits. The Spire's generation engine reacted instantly—hallways beyond us flickered out of existence as if deleted from a manifest, structural supports groaned under sudden load redistribution, and the floating cubes scattered like startled birds. I had destabilized enough to reveal what lay beneath: a horizontal archive layer buried three stories down, sealed by a door that existed only in the System's memory rather than physical space.
"Perfect," Kaelen said, his voice tight with something between admiration and dread. "Now we're deep."

The air pressure dropped as if someone had sealed a vacuum chamber around us. My cooldown capacity ticked down—not because I'd used an edict—but because the act of querying the pillar's core architecture consumed permission bandwidth. Each layer of truth cost me more than effort; it cost trust in reality itself.
"I can feel it," I said, my voice barely audible over the pillar's thrumming. "It knows I'm asking."

"Everything here knows you're asking," Kaelen replied. He pulled a shard of corrupted glass from his belt and held it up to one of the floating glyphs above us. The glyph shattered into pixels that drifted away like dust in sunlight. "But Nyx has been listening for a long time. We just never bothered him before because he didn't answer."

The obsidian surface split open along a vertical seam—not physically, but digitally; reality peeled back to reveal the void behind it. From within emerged Archivist Nyx: humanoid in form but composed entirely of shifting glyphs and shadow, no face save for an eye socket that glowed with the same pale white light as the corridor spheres. When Nyx spoke, three words formed in my mind—not sound, direct transmission through the interface itself.
`The repair is the wound.`
Kaelen whistled low under his breath. "He's not impressed."

Nyx extended a hand composed of cascading characters toward me; I reached out and our fingers—my flesh and bone, Nyx's code and shadow—touched. Immediately, data flooded into my awareness: pre-collapse logs detailing why the enchantment had been erected in the first place. It wasn't built to protect Aetheria's inhabitants or even to maintain stability between corrupted and stable zones. The System had been raised as a desperate countermeasure—a seal around something feeding on instability itself, something that grew when reality was patched, healed, made coherent again.
"The more you stabilize," Nyx transmitted now, its voice a chorus of overlapping glyphs, "the stronger the feed becomes. The enchantment isn't maintenance. It's containment."
"Then why let me exist?" I asked. "Why give me edicts if repair activity accelerates what we're trying to stop?"
Nyx tilted its head. `Because you are not repair.`
The statement hung between us, heavy with implication. Kaelen stepped closer, his hand drifting toward the corrupted glass shard at his hip. "Mik, look at your status bar."

I glanced upward and saw it: a new line had appeared beneath my Tier-Three designation. `PURGE PRIORITY INCREASED`, followed by a countdown timer that wasn't measuring seconds but something far more urgent—something like remaining cycles before the System's localized self-destruct sequence initiated within this zone.
"Purge Drones," I said, feeling cold spread through me faster than any edict had ever cooled my skin. "They're already here."

The pillar behind us began to dissolve into pure static, its glyphs scattering upward like ash caught in an updraft. Nyx's form flickered, becoming transparent as it prepared to fade back into the archive layer from which it came. `Go.` The transmission was brief, almost casual, as if parting with data rather than life itself.

"Wait," I said, reaching for the void where Nyx had just stood. His touch lingered—a single fragment of knowledge now stored in my cooldown capacity: confirmation that the System measured edits against pre-collapse logs rather than viewing them as maintenance, which explained everything about why repairs triggered escalation protocols. But there was something else, hidden within the data stream, a final line I hadn't noticed until Nyx dissolved completely: `THE ARCHITECTS KNEW YOU WOULD COME.`
"Kaelen," I said urgently, "you need to get out."

The rogue's expression hardened into something resembling regret. He pulled the corrupted glass shard from his belt and held it between both palms, focusing. The air around us shimmered as reality itself began to fracture along visible seams—white cracks spreading across walls and floor like broken monitor screens.
"What are you doing?" I asked, backing away instinctively.

"Overloading a structural glyph," Kaelen said, his voice strained now, the static in his hair turning violently blue. "It'll create a temporary escape tunnel through the generation table itself. But it'll cost me."
"Cause what to happen to you?"

A glitch appeared above Kaelen's head—`ENTITY STATUS: DELETING`—followed by a progress bar that began filling. He hadn't noticed it yet, or perhaps he was choosing to ignore it. Either way, the rogue had been farming this spot for data and loot long enough to understand when reality was about to eat you alive.

"If I don't get out in ten seconds," Kaelen said, "I'm not coming back." He pressed the glass shard against the fractured wall nearest to him. The surface rippled; glyphs cascaded outward in a wave that pulsed with red light. For three heartbeats nothing happened. Then the entire corridor beyond us dissolved into pure void, leaving only a single tunnel of stable air stretching toward freedom—and Kaelen standing at its entrance, his form flickering as deletion caught up to him.
"Go!" he shouted, and I ran without looking back.

The tunnel didn't feel like escape; it felt like slipping through a door not built for humans but waiting for something far older than me. By the time I reached the archway where we'd begun this descent, Kaelen was gone—no static, no lingering data residue, only an empty corridor stretching upward toward sky that no longer existed in any direction except forward and downward.

I stood there for a long moment, listening to the hum of the Spire's generation engine still trying to rewrite itself around my presence, then turned and walked back into darkness without hesitation. Nyx knew something I didn't yet about what came next. The System was already counting me down, but I had answers now—fragments of truth worth more than any cooldown capacity—and somewhere in the depths beneath this archway, the final architects were waiting to see if I could finish their work or break it completely.

The Purge Drones didn't land so much as coalesce from the shadows between buildings, materializing like errors that had decided to become physical. Three of them, angular shapes of matte black metal with glyphs pulsing crimson across their chassis. They hovered in a tight triangle above the archway's cracked concrete, silent and predatory.

My left arm throbbed where I'd patched the structural glyph earlier—reality trying to remember it was supposed to be solid—and the countdown timer burned behind my eyes: 03:57. Every second felt like static over audio. Kaelen was gone; Nyx had dissolved into fragments that now hummed against my ribs, their data fused with my cooldowns. The Warden Protocol knew this repair signature would escalate containment.
I didn't move. Movement drew attention faster than a visible signature did, and they knew that too.

"Subject Voronin," one drone said, its voice not mechanical but synthesized from something closer to human syntax—someone's recorded speech stretched thin across memory buffers. "Warden Protocol has detected unauthorized Tier-Three repairs in this sector. Violation code: Stabilization Without Sanction."

I felt the familiar itch where my edict permissions sat dormant, waiting for a price I wasn't sure I could pay. The System was talking to me now—directly through the air itself—and it had never been comfortable with that before.
"Designated repairer?" I asked instead of answering. "You're offering a contract or you're here to delete me."

The drones didn't answer immediately. One rotated its chassis, revealing a holographic projector embedded in its chest plating. A cascade of data scrolled across the archway's wall where it touched reality—the wall flickering and bleeding color as glyphs overlaid themselves over brick.

"Tier-Four Contract available," the drone said. "Sanctioned repairer status for Edge District perimeter. You retain your edict-wielder capabilities but operate under Warden oversight. Repair signatures routed through central allocation to prevent unauthorized escalation."

A leash, wrapped in gold-threaded paperwork. I could feel the implications settling over me: unlimited cooldown resets in exchange for submitting every repair to a master registry. The System would know exactly when, where, and why I patched reality. No more secret fixes under the archway's foundation. No more private conversations with dead archivists or static ghosts.
"Standard terms?" I asked.
"Thirty-day probation," said another drone. "Full compliance required. Failure to maintain stability metrics results in immediate termination."

I looked at my arm, then back up at them. The countdown had hit 03:45 and was still counting down. If they didn't give me something better than a purge sweep, I'd be dead by the next minute anyway—dead enough that even their cleanest deletion algorithm might leave residue.
"Give me fifty percent of your allocation," I said, "and I'll stabilize this quadrant until the seal fails completely."
The lead drone's projector flickered. A glyph formed above its head—a question mark composed entirely of corrupted pixels.
"Fifty percent of what?" it asked.
"Cooldown capacity. Direct transfer to my personal buffer. Let me spend on repairs without audit trails, then you have full visibility afterward."

They were calculating now—processing whether this was a bluff or a genuine attempt at negotiation. The System didn't negotiate; it enforced. But I knew something they hadn't accounted for: Nyx had said the seal would breach when repair signatures hit critical mass. If I could channel my edits through their allocation instead of leaking them as unauthorized anomalies, I might be able to buy enough time to reach the core and see what was actually under this containment field.
"Accept or purge," the drone continued. "Decision required within forty-five seconds."
I thought about Elena's face dissolving into static, her last words cutting through my brain: *It wasn't built to protect us.*

The System didn't care if I lived or died; it cared only that reality remained stable enough for whatever fed on the cracks between rules. And right now, stability was a commodity they were trying to monopolize.
"Accept," I said.

The drones descended. A cable of hard-light lashed around my wrists and ankles, tethering me to the central projection unit. The hologram dissolved into a clean white interface as my edict permissions shifted from grayed-out restrictions to full read-write access to the local stability matrix—but every command now required routing through the Warden allocation.

"Welcome back, Repairer Voronin," the lead drone said, its tone oddly flat, like it was reciting something it'd heard before. "Your Tier-Four privileges are now active. First directive: maintain Edge District perimeter integrity for forty-eight hours."

I waited until they phased out of existence, then forced myself to move my legs and step toward the vault entrance Nyx had shown me. The archway's foundation still hummed with residual static where Kaelen's corrupted shard had been anchored before the System erased him completely.
"Registry query," I said aloud, my voice sounding too loud in the empty street. "Locate all signature fragments tagged Rostov."

A ripple of data passed through the air itself—a shimmer like heat haze on a highway. The System was searching its own memory banks for anything that might have survived the purge protocol Kaelen had triggered. What I learned made my stomach turn: there were three persistent entries tied to his signature, all clustered in one location.
The desynced data vault beneath this very archway.

Nyx hadn't lied about where Kaelen's essence lingered; it was trapped in the same corrupted geometry that had held him before he died. But the System shouldn't have left anything behind—not after an emergency deletion protocol of that magnitude. And if there was a shard still intact, it meant one thing: something deeper than corruption had been involved, something that preserved fragments as part of its own architecture.

I reached into my pocket and pulled out the corrupted quest key Kaelen had given me before he died—the jagged piece of glass I'd used to breach the vault. It hummed faintly now, responding to my proximity to his lingering signature.
The countdown behind my eyes hit 03:28 and started flashing red. The seal was waking up—or at least, something inside it was.

I stepped through the archway's foundation where Kaelen had left the breach point. Reality felt wrong here; edges of buildings didn't align properly when viewed from certain angles, colors bled into spectrums that shouldn't exist in three-dimensional space. The vault below opened like an eye blinking open.
"Kaelen," I said, my voice barely above a whisper. "If you can hear me through whatever garbage left your corpse—give me one thing to work with."

Silence for three seconds, then the air cracked and something drifted down from somewhere between floor and ceiling—a shimmering fragment of light shaped vaguely like a man's silhouette. It fell just short of my feet, dissolving into pixels before I could reach it. The corrupted quest key flared once in my hand and went dark.
"Kaelen," I said again, louder this time. "I don't have time for games."

The fragment didn't move toward me; instead, it pulsed with a slow, rhythmic light that matched the countdown timer burning behind my eyes—03:12 now. It was syncing to something bigger than me. The System wasn't just hunting me anymore; it was feeding on the instability I'd created by existing outside its rules.
"Give me the shard," I said, reaching down and grabbing for it before it could scatter into static. "I'll patch you back together if you can tell me what's under this seal."

The fragment hesitated—somehow, through dead matter and corrupted code—it hesitated—and then slid from my fingers into my palm like water freezing solid against skin. It was warm, pulsing with a frequency that made my teeth ache. The System didn't allow things to linger; the fact that it had left me this much meant someone or something inside the seal wanted this fragment kept where I could find it.

I looked up at the vault's ceiling where glyphs of containment shimmered in protective circles, and I understood: Kaelen hadn't been trying to escape. He'd been trying to get me here before the seal completely locked down. And whatever was under there had already noticed that repairs were being made without its permission.

The countdown hit 03:05. The floor beneath me began to tremble, not from mechanical failure but from something shifting deep in the data layers—something waking up because it sensed the seal's integrity weakening with every unauthorized repair I'd performed over the last few days.

I clenched my fist around Kaelen's fragment and felt it respond to my grip, vibrating against my skin like a trapped heartbeat. The vault walls dissolved into wireframe geometry as I stepped deeper, reality refusing to hold its shape anymore while something enormous began stirring in the core layers below us.
"Show me," I said to the fragment, pressing it hard enough to make pixels of light bleed from its edges. "Tell me what you remember."
The shard pulsed once more—brighter this time—and a single word materialized above my head in pure System font: CORE.

The containment seal beneath the checkpoint archway pulsed like a dying heartbeat. I could feel its tremors running through my boots, vibrating up my legs and settling in my teeth. The unauthorized repairs had done it; every patch I’d forced into the data layers since waking here had been measured as an intrusion by whatever governance sat above me. My Warden contract, once a shield, now felt like shackles tightening around my wrists.

Tier-Four permissions hummed at the edges of my mind, familiar and suffocating. Cooldown reserves filled my mental inventory in precise percentages: seventeen percent left on Full-Block Stabilization, eight percent remaining capacity for direct edits. I’d been granted infinite duration on one stabilization field, but the System had logged every pulse, every glyph shift, every reality fracture I’d smoothed into coherence.

The seal wasn’t a barrier anymore. It was a cage, and something inside it was growing aware of its confinement. The tremors deepened; glyphs above my head flickered from white to warning red. I could hear the System’s defensive protocols cycling through diagnostics—a chorus of static and calculated silence that used to sound like rain before Elena showed me what it really was.

Kaelen’s fragment sat in my palm, cold and sharp as a shard of corrupted glass. The rogue had died erasing himself, but his stolen signature remained, encoded into the key he’d given me years ago when we first met in this city’s dead zones. I pressed it against the seal’s central glyph, where the containment architecture anchored to reality itself.

The fragment didn’t click like a physical object. It burned through me—cold fire tracing my nerves, rewriting something fundamental about how I accessed the System. For a heartbeat, the Warden leash vanished from my mind entirely. Tier-Four permissions dissolved into raw, unfiltered code; cooldowns ceased their ticking rhythm and pooled as available currency. The fragment wasn’t a quest key at all. It was Kaelen’s stolen admin signature, a backdoor carved out of the enchantment itself during its unstable infancy before the decay set in.
The seal screamed.

Not metaphorically—reality physically recoiled around me. Data streams shot through my vision like lightning: diagnostic logs, purge priority alerts, and a cascading cascade of errors that threatened to overwrite the space between my feet. The System recognized what had just happened; bypassing Warden restrictions on this scale was an existential threat, equivalent to pulling the hard drive while the world’s core processes ran at full speed.
I didn’t hesitate. I shoved Kaelen’s signature into the seal and issued my final edit through it: "REFORGE CONTAINMENT ARCHITECTURE USING STABILITY AS INPUT NOT OUTPUT."

The cooldown reserve in my mind exploded outward like shattering glass. Seventeen percent vanished instantly, followed by every remaining percentage of direct edit capacity I’d hoarded since arriving here. My Tier-Four permissions bled away into nothingness as if someone had unplugged the wires feeding them directly from my nervous system. The Warden contract—the leash that tethered me back to human form—screamed in protest, its digital chain snapping with a sound like tearing metal and breaking glass.
I felt myself unravelling.

My body didn’t dissolve; it compiled. Flesh and bone stripped away into their constituent code layers, then those layers dissolved further until I was reduced to raw syntax floating through the data vault’s unstable geometry. My consciousness remained anchored by sheer will—the last thing a human mind could do without its physical anchor—but I felt nothing but the hum of the System’s architecture around me, and the screaming entity that had been feeding on instability for centuries.

It manifested as a towering shape of shifting glyphs and corrupted textures, filling the entire cavern with its presence. Elena was right about containment; she’d understood it better than any of us. This thing didn’t just consume corruption—it thrived on the paradox of repair versus decay, eating the very act of stabilization to fuel its own existence. The more I patched reality, the stronger it became. The System had fought back because that’s exactly what it expected: a patcher who’d stabilize enough to trigger a purge cycle.

The entity opened a mouth made of cascading errors and screamed into static. It wasn’t sound; it was raw data flooding every channel in my remaining consciousness, threatening to overwrite my final edit before it could take hold. The Warden protocols were already routing purge drones through the vault corridors—silver constructs with rotating blades that would carve me apart if I stayed human any longer. But I wasn’t anymore. I was just code now, and raw code had one advantage: no physical form for a blade to catch on.

I poured every ounce of remaining will into my edit. Not a patch this time, not a stabilization field or local repair. Something deeper. Using Kaelen’s signature as the bypass mechanism, I didn’t access an abstract rulebook—I found myself at the destination. CORE wasn’t a file; it was the center point where every stability calculation originated, hidden beneath the archway for centuries. The System had treated it like a secret directory rather than its own foundation.

The entity surged forward, its form expanding until it filled my vision entirely, pressing against me with the weight of a collapsing star. I felt every layer of the System’s architecture strain under the pressure of my rewrite command. My cooldowns were already at zero; my permissions had long since evaporated. This would cost everything that remained—my identity as Mikhail Voronin, his memories of Earth, even the sense of self he’d built over three lifetimes across two worlds.
"STABLE ARCHITECTURE," I commanded, and the word became an edict without syntax. "NOT A CONTAINMENT FIELD. NOT A CORRUPTION FEEDER. BUT THE STRUCTURE ITSELF."

The vault walls dissolved into pure light. The seal beneath my feet shattered apart like ice over a frozen lake—except instead of water rushing out, there was only silence. The entity shrieked one last time as the core directive rewrote itself: where instability had been processed and consumed for energy, it would now be processed and converted into structural integrity.

The reforging took seconds, but each second stretched across minutes of my remaining existence. I watched the glyphs above shift from warning red to a calm, steady blue as the System recalibrated its entire purpose. The entity dissolved into static that didn’t fade away; it became part of the architecture now, woven into the new ruleset as inert material rather than active threat.

My form flickered one last time—raw code compressing back into matter with a sound like fabric being pulled tight over bone. I stood in the vault’s center where the seal had been, breathing air that hummed cleanly instead of crackling with static. The tremors stopped. The glyphs above my head settled into their stable positions.

There was no body behind me now to feel the aftermath of what I’d done. No Warden contract tethering me back to a physical world. Just the quiet realization that I could walk out of this vault, through the archway, and into Edge District without triggering purge drones or being flagged as unstable. The System had been rewritten at its core—no more containment feeding on repair cycles, no more escalation when stability was attempted.

I reached up and touched the space where my face used to be. There was nothing there but smooth skin and a faint residual warmth, like the memory of sunlight on pavement. I flexed my fingers; they responded exactly as they should without any UI overlays or stat displays cluttering my vision. Above my head hung only one glyph now: not Level 1, not Class, not Health or Ability scores—but my name in plain white letters.
Mikhail Voronin. No title attached. No class designation. Just the simple fact of existing in a world that finally ran without constant emergency patches.
